eSVD2: master (3d5f7bf) versus devel (1.1.0) on simulated cohorts

Drafted by Claude for Kevin Z. Lin

2026-09-29

library(ggplot2)
out_dir <- "output"
version_vec <- c("master", "devel", "devel_swap")

gene_df <- do.call(rbind, lapply(version_vec, function(v){
  utils::read.csv(file.path(out_dir, v, "genes.csv"))
}))
truth_df <- utils::read.csv(file.path(out_dir, "truth.csv"))
gene_df <- merge(gene_df, truth_df, by = c("regime", "rep", "gene"))
gene_df$p <- 10^(-gene_df$log10p)
gene_df$status <- factor(ifelse(gene_df$is_de, "DE", "null"),
                         levels = c("null", "DE"))

run_df <- do.call(rbind, lapply(version_vec, function(v){
  utils::read.csv(file.path(out_dir, v, "runs.csv"))
}))
corner_df <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("master", "devel"), function(v){
  utils::read.csv(file.path(out_dir, v, "corner_cases.csv"))
}))
wall_time_df <- utils::read.csv(file.path(out_dir, "wall_time.csv"),
                                header = FALSE)

# One row per gene per data set, with the versions side by side.
.wide <- function(column){
  master_df <- gene_df[gene_df$version == "master",
                       c("regime", "rep", "gene", "status", column)]
  devel_df <- gene_df[gene_df$version == "devel",
                      c("regime", "rep", "gene", column)]
  swap_df <- gene_df[gene_df$version == "devel_swap",
                     c("regime", "rep", "gene", column)]
  colnames(master_df)[5] <- "master"
  colnames(devel_df)[4] <- "devel"
  colnames(swap_df)[4] <- "devel_swap"
  res <- merge(master_df, devel_df, by = c("regime", "rep", "gene"))
  merge(res, swap_df, by = c("regime", "rep", "gene"))
}

regime_levels <- c("baseline", "null", "strong_de", "near_poisson",
                   "minimal_design", "generate_null")
version_col_vec <- c(master = "#2a78d6", devel = "#eb6834",
                     devel_swap = "#1baf7a")
status_col_vec <- c(null = "#9e9d97", DE = "#4a3aa7")

theme_set(theme_bw(base_size = 11))
theme_update(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
             strip.background = element_rect(fill = "#f1f0ec", colour = NA))
num_null_genes <- sum(!gene_df$is_de & gene_df$version == "master" &
                        gene_df$regime == "null") / 10
.fp_per_rep <- function(v, r){
  idx <- gene_df$version == v & gene_df$regime == r
  sum(gene_df$fdr[idx] < 0.05 & !gene_df$is_de[idx]) / 10
}
.type1 <- function(v, r){
  idx <- gene_df$version == v & gene_df$regime == r & !gene_df$is_de
  mean(gene_df$p[idx] < 0.05)
}
logfc_wide_df <- .wide("logFC")
min_logfc_cor <- min(sapply(split(logfc_wide_df, logfc_wide_df$regime),
                            function(x){stats::cor(x$master, x$devel)}))
teststat_wide_df <- .wide("teststat")
swap_cor <- stats::cor(teststat_wide_df$master, teststat_wide_df$devel_swap)

1 Overview

This report compares two versions of eSVD2 on the same simulated data:

  • master: git commit 3d5f7bf, DESCRIPTION version 1.0.1.07. This is what devtools::install_github("linnykos/eSVD2") installs today.
  • devel: the working tree on the devel branch (commit d49e402), version 1.1.0, the candidate for CRAN.

It asks two questions. Which behaviors got better? And did the rewrite change what eSVD-DE reports on ordinary data, or mostly how it behaves at the edges?

The short answer.

  1. The point estimate did not change. The log2 fold changes of the two versions agree at a Pearson correlation of at least 0.9982 in every regime.
  2. Most of the fixes are corner-case fixes, and they behave as NEWS.md says. Inputs that used to crash deep in the optimizer with missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed, or finish silently with a wrong answer, now stop at the first step with a message that names the problem (section 7).
  3. One change does move ordinary results: the overdispersion estimator (gamma_rate). It changes every gene’s nuisance rate, so it changes every Welch statistic and p-value. Replacing devel’s nuisance estimates with master’s reproduces master’s Welch statistics at correlation 1.0000 (section 5.3). In these simulations the new estimator ranks genes by their true overdispersion far better than the old one, but it produces more false discoveries. Under the global null, 2.7 of 300 null genes per data set reach FDR < 0.05, against 0.2 under master. In the near-Poisson regime the type-I error at p < 0.05 is 0.28 against 0.07. This is a dramatic change, and it is not an improvement (section 6).

1.1 How the comparison was run

The two versions are installed into separate private libraries and run in separate R processes. The step-by-step API (initialize_esvd() through compute_pvalue()) has the same function names and arguments in both, so one script drives either version, calling the steps in the order eSVD() runs them. All heavy computation happens in the scripts; this document only reads their CSVs.

Script What it does
00_install_versions_claude.sh git archive 3d5f7bf → lib/master; the working tree → lib/devel
helpers_claude.R the simulator and the pipeline, shared by the scripts below
01_simulate_data_claude.R 6 regimes × 10 replicates → data/*.rds, and the truth → output/truth.csv
02_run_regimes_claude.R fits all 60 data sets with one version → output/<version>/genes.csv, runs.csv
03_corner_cases_claude.R 12 perturbed cohorts per version → output/<version>/corner_cases.csv
run_all_claude.sh all of the above, end to end

The whole of run_all_claude.sh took 6.4 minutes on the laptop it was run on.

devel_swap is an ablation, not a third version. It runs the devel code on each data set, but right after estimate_nuisance() it overwrites the per-gene nuisance rate with the value master estimated on the same data set. Where devel_swap matches master, the nuisance estimate explains the difference between the versions.

1.2 The simulated regimes

Every regime has 20 individuals (10 case, 10 control), 30 cells each, and 300 genes. Except for generate_null, the data come from the eSVD hierarchical model itself, using the generator of .build_tiny_data() in tests/testthat/helper-fixtures.R. That model has a rank-3 latent structure, an individual-level random effect, Sex and Age effects, a per-cell library size, and counts \(A_{ji} \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\ell_{ji} \lambda_{ji})\) with \(\lambda_{ji} \sim \mathrm{Gamma}(\text{mean} = \mu_{ji}, \text{rate} = \beta_j)\). The truth for a gene’s log2 fold change is the ratio of the arithmetic means of \(\exp(\text{natural parameter})\) in the two arms, which is what both the logFC and the Welch statistic contrast.

Regime DE genes Nuisance rate \(\beta_j\) What it probes
baseline 15, effect 0.8 (natural log) U(2, 8) on the log scale ordinary data
null 0 U(2, 8) calibration
strong_de 15, effect ±3 U(2, 8) large Welch statistics; the t → z mapping
near_poisson 15, effect 0.8 U(50, 1000) little overdispersion; the old gamma_rate cap
minimal_design 15, effect 0.8 U(2, 8) no Sex/Age, so covariates are only Intercept + Log_UMI + CC (the GLM-fallback offset fix)
generate_null 10 the package’s own generate_null() a generator not written for this report

Each regime has 10 replicates with different seeds. The fit uses k = 3, l2pen = 0.1, max_iter = 50, and otherwise the package defaults.

2 What changed, according to NEWS.md

Change in devel Where this report looks at it
Welch → Gaussian mapping done on the log scale, so a large statistic no longer becomes Inf 6.4
multtest() reports its empirical-null estimator and warns on the locfdr fallback; Efron’s truncated MLE regains p0 <= 1 6.5, 7
gamma_rate no longer caps its search at the largest library size 4, 5, 6
initialize_esvd() refuses all-zero genes; zeroes NA in sparse input 7
GLM fallback (≤ 1 covariate besides intercept and offsets) keeps the library-size offset 3, regime minimal_design
Collinear covariates refused by name 7
eSVD() refuses individuals in both arms, one-individual arms, and individuals with too few cells 7
Iterative SVD starts from a fixed vector (determinism) 7
New: log2fc_vec, log2fc_se_vec, compute_log_fold_change() 8

3 Point estimates: the log2 fold change

plot_df <- logfc_wide_df
plot_df$regime <- factor(plot_df$regime, levels = regime_levels)
plot1 <- ggplot2::ggplot(plot_df, ggplot2::aes(x = master, y = devel))
plot1 <- plot1 + ggplot2::geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0,
                                      colour = "#c3c2b7", linewidth = 0.5)
plot1 <- plot1 + ggplot2::geom_point(ggplot2::aes(colour = status),
                                     size = 0.8, alpha = 0.6)
plot1 <- plot1 + ggplot2::facet_wrap(~ regime, nrow = 2, scales = "free")
plot1 <- plot1 + ggplot2::scale_colour_manual(values = status_col_vec,
                                              name = "True status")
plot1 <- plot1 + ggplot2::labs(x = "master: log2 fold change",
                               y = "devel: log2 fold change",
                               title = "The log2 fold change is essentially unchanged",
                               subtitle = "All 10 replicates per regime; grey line is y = x")
plot(plot1)

agreement_df <- do.call(rbind, lapply(regime_levels, function(r){
  x <- logfc_wide_df[logfc_wide_df$regime == r, ]
  data.frame(regime = r,
             pearson = stats::cor(x$master, x$devel),
             median_abs_diff = stats::median(abs(x$master - x$devel)),
             max_abs_diff = max(abs(x$master - x$devel)))
}))
knitr::kable(agreement_df, digits = 4,
             col.names = c("Regime", "Pearson r", "Median |Δ|", "Max |Δ|"),
             caption = "log2 fold change, master vs devel, all genes and replicates.")
log2 fold change, master vs devel, all genes and replicates.
Regime Pearson r Median |Δ| Max |Δ|
baseline 0.9998 0.0019 0.0291
null 0.9990 0.0020 0.0306
strong_de 1.0000 0.0021 0.0775
near_poisson 0.9982 0.0093 0.1256
minimal_design 0.9999 0.0015 0.0269
generate_null 1.0000 0.0001 0.0417

The logFC is log2(case_mean / control_mean), where each mean averages the per-individual posterior means. The posterior mean moves only a little with the nuisance rate, so this estimate is nearly identical across versions. The small differences come from the fit and from the rescaling by bool_stabilize_underdispersion. devel returns this quantity directly as log2fc_vec; for master it is computed from case_mean and control_mean. The two definitions are the same.

minimal_design is where the GLM-fallback offset fix would show, and it does not. With only Intercept + Log_UMI + CC, master fitted the intercepts without the depth offset. That changes the initialization, but after two rounds of opt_esvd() the fold changes agree as closely as in any other regime.

4 The nuisance (overdispersion) estimate

nuisance_vec is the Gamma rate \(\beta_j = 1/\gamma_j\): a large value means little overdispersion, and \(\beta_j \to \infty\) is a Poisson gene.

4.1 Against the truth

plot_df <- gene_df[gene_df$version %in% c("master", "devel") &
                     gene_df$regime != "generate_null", ]
plot_df$regime <- factor(plot_df$regime, levels = regime_levels)
plot_df$version <- factor(plot_df$version, levels = c("master", "devel"))
plot1 <- ggplot2::ggplot(plot_df, ggplot2::aes(x = nuisance_true, y = nuisance))
plot1 <- plot1 + ggplot2::geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0,
                                      colour = "#52514e", linewidth = 0.5,
                                      linetype = "dashed")
plot1 <- plot1 + ggplot2::geom_point(ggplot2::aes(colour = version),
                                     size = 0.7, alpha = 0.45)
plot1 <- plot1 + ggplot2::facet_grid(version ~ regime, scales = "free_x")
plot1 <- plot1 + ggplot2::scale_x_log10()
plot1 <- plot1 + ggplot2::scale_y_log10()
plot1 <- plot1 + ggplot2::scale_colour_manual(values = version_col_vec,
                                              guide = "none")
plot1 <- plot1 + ggplot2::labs(x = "True rate (log scale)",
                               y = "Estimated rate (log scale)",
                               title = "master's estimate carries no information about the truth; devel's ranks it but diverges",
                               subtitle = "Dashed line is y = x. Points near 1e7 are devel estimates that ran off to the upper end of the search.")
plot(plot1)

nuisance_acc_df <- do.call(rbind, lapply(setdiff(regime_levels, "generate_null"),
                                         function(r){
  do.call(rbind, lapply(c("master", "devel"), function(v){
    x <- gene_df[gene_df$regime == r & gene_df$version == v, ]
    data.frame(regime = r,
               version = v,
               spearman = stats::cor(x$nuisance, x$nuisance_true,
                                     method = "spearman"),
               median_ratio = stats::median(x$nuisance / x$nuisance_true),
               max_estimate = max(x$nuisance),

  }))
}))

What the plot and table show:

  • master’s estimates are nearly independent of the truth (Spearman near 0) and never exceed a few tens: the old search interval ended at the largest library size. Even in near_poisson, where the true rates are 50 to 1000, master reports rates in the single digits and tens. It therefore treats every gene as moderately overdispersed.
  • devel ranks the genes correctly (Spearman about 0.6 when the truth is U(2, 8)), but it is biased upward two- to threefold, and some estimates diverge. About 0.5% of ordinary genes, and about half of the near_poisson genes, land near \(10^7\). This is Q10 / Q-LFC-1 in CLAUDE_kevin.md, now with a measured consequence.

4.2 Why the nuisance matters downstream

The posterior shrinks each cell’s observed count toward the fitted mean with weight governed by \(\beta_j\). A huge \(\beta_j\) makes the posterior collapse onto the fitted mean. The within-individual posterior variance then vanishes, the denominator of the Welch statistic shrinks, and the statistic grows. The next section follows that chain through to the p-values.

The Pearson correlations in the second column understate the agreement for most genes. The typical gene moves little (median |Δ| in the third column), and the correlation is pulled down by the few genes that move a great deal.

5.3 The ablation: the nuisance estimate is the whole difference

The table’s third column is the decisive one. Put master’s nuisance rates into the devel code and the Welch statistics match master’s in every regime: to within 0.006, and to all six stored digits in four of the six regimes. The other changes between the versions (the reparameterization by QR, the offset in the GLM fallback, the deterministic SVD start, the rewritten empirical-null estimators) move nothing that reaches the statistic in these regimes. Everything that differs between the versions’ Welch statistics comes from the one line that changed gamma_rate’s search interval.

plot_df <- teststat_wide_df[teststat_wide_df$regime %in%
                              c("baseline", "null", "near_poisson"), ]
plot_df$regime <- factor(plot_df$regime, levels = regime_levels)
plot1 <- ggplot2::ggplot(plot_df, ggplot2::aes(x = master, y = devel_swap))
plot1 <- plot1 + ggplot2::geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0,
                                      colour = "#c3c2b7", linewidth = 0.5)
plot1 <- plot1 + ggplot2::geom_point(colour = version_col_vec[["devel_swap"]],
                                     size = 0.8, alpha = 0.6)
plot1 <- plot1 + ggplot2::facet_wrap(~ regime, nrow = 1, scales = "free")
plot1 <- plot1 + ggplot2::labs(x = "master: Welch statistic",
                               y = "devel with master's nuisance: Welch statistic",
                               title = "devel_swap reproduces master exactly")
plot(plot1)

6 Calibration and power

6.1 Null genes: p-value QQ plots

The p-values below are the ones each version reports, measured against its estimated empirical null. Each panel pools the null genes of all 10 replicates.

qq_list <- list()
for(r in regime_levels){
  for(v in c("master", "devel")){
    p_vec <- gene_df$p[gene_df$regime == r & gene_df$version == v &
                         !gene_df$is_de]
    p_vec <- sort(p_vec)
    qq_list[[paste(r, v)]] <- data.frame(regime = r,
                                         version = v,
                                         expected = -log10(stats::ppoints(length(p_vec))),
                                         observed = -log10(p_vec))
  }
}
qq_df <- do.call(rbind, qq_list)
qq_df$regime <- factor(qq_df$regime, levels = regime_levels)
qq_df$version <- factor(qq_df$version, levels = c("master", "devel"))
plot1 <- ggplot2::ggplot(qq_df, ggplot2::aes(x = expected, y = observed))
plot1 <- plot1 + ggplot2::geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0,
                                      colour = "#52514e", linewidth = 0.5,
                                      linetype = "dashed")
plot1 <- plot1 + ggplot2::geom_point(ggplot2::aes(colour = version),
                                     size = 0.8, alpha = 0.7)
plot1 <- plot1 + ggplot2::facet_wrap(~ regime, nrow = 2, scales = "free_y")
plot1 <- plot1 + ggplot2::scale_colour_manual(values = version_col_vec,
                                              name = "Version")
plot1 <- plot1 + ggplot2::labs(x = "Expected −log10 p (uniform)",
                               y = "Observed −log10 p, null genes",
                               title = "devel's null p-values have a heavier upper tail; near_poisson is badly miscalibrated")
plot(plot1)

6.2 False and true discoveries at FDR < 0.05

discovery_df <- do.call(rbind, lapply(regime_levels, function(r){
  do.call(rbind, lapply(version_vec, function(v){
    x <- gene_df[gene_df$regime == r & gene_df$version == v, ]
    sig_vec <- x$fdr < 0.05
    data.frame(regime = r,
               version = v,
               type1 = mean(x$p[!x$is_de] < 0.05),
               fp = sum(sig_vec & !x$is_de) / 10,
               tp = sum(sig_vec & x$is_de) / 10,
               num_de = sum(x$is_de) / 10,
               fdp = sum(sig_vec & !x$is_de) / max(1, sum(sig_vec)))
  }))
}))

fp_list <- list()
for(r in regime_levels){
  for(v in c("master", "devel")){
    for(i in 1:10){
      idx <- gene_df$regime == r & gene_df$version == v & gene_df$rep == i
      fp_list[[paste(r, v, i)]] <- data.frame(regime = r,
                                              version = v,
                                              rep = i,
                                              fp = sum(gene_df$fdr[idx] < 0.05 &
                                                         !gene_df$is_de[idx]))
    }
  }
}

plot1 <- ggplot2::ggplot(fp_df, ggplot2::aes(x = version, y = fp + 1))

plot1 <- plot1 + ggplot2::labs(x = NULL,
                               y = "False discoveries + 1 (log scale)",
                               title = "False discoveries per data set at FDR < 0.05",
                               subtitle = "One point per replicate")
plot(plot1)

What this shows:

  • At p < 0.05 the null genes are calibrated in both versions in the ordinary regimes (type-I error 0.04 to 0.06). The empirical null absorbs most of the shift in the statistics.
  • The difference is in the far tail, which is where FDR control acts. devel’s null statistics have a heavier upper tail, so a few null genes per data set pass BH. About a quarter to a half of those (all of them in near_poisson) are genes whose nuisance rate diverged (section 6.3). The rest reflect the general upward bias of devel’s rates.
  • near_poisson is badly miscalibrated under devel: about 60 of 285 null genes per data set are declared DE, and power also drops. In that regime about half the genes’ rates diverge, the empirical null is fitted to a mixture of collapsed and uncollapsed genes, and neither group is scored correctly.
  • master is not “right” here either. Its rates ignore the truth, but treating every gene as moderately overdispersed happens to be conservative, so its errors are errors of caution.

6.3 Where devel’s false discoveries come from

A diverged rate is close to a guaranteed false discovery. In the ordinary regimes, 74% to 100% of the null genes whose rate diverged reach FDR < 0.05, against under 1% of the others (table below). The divergence is rare (about 0.5% of genes), but each occurrence is almost always an error.

plot_df <- gene_df[gene_df$version == "devel" &
                     gene_df$regime %in% c("null", "near_poisson"), ]
plot_df$regime <- factor(plot_df$regime, levels = regime_levels)
plot_df$discovery <- ifelse(plot_df$fdr < 0.05, "FDR < 0.05", "not significant")
plot1 <- ggplot2::ggplot(plot_df, ggplot2::aes(x = nuisance, y = abs(teststat)))
plot1 <- plot1 + ggplot2::geom_point(ggplot2::aes(colour = discovery,
                                                  shape = status),
                                     size = 1.2, alpha = 0.7)
plot1 <- plot1 + ggplot2::facet_wrap(~ regime, nrow = 1, scales = "free_y")
plot1 <- plot1 + ggplot2::scale_x_log10()
plot1 <- plot1 + ggplot2::scale_colour_manual(values = c(`FDR < 0.05` = "#eb6834",
                                                         `not significant` = "#9e9d97"),
                                              name = NULL)
plot1 <- plot1 + ggplot2::scale_shape_manual(values = c(null = 16, DE = 17),
                                             name = "True status")
plot1 <- plot1 + ggplot2::labs(x = "devel: estimated nuisance rate (log scale)",
                               y = "|Welch statistic|",
                               title = "A diverged rate (right-hand cluster) inflates the Welch statistic")
plot(plot1)

devel_df <- gene_df[gene_df$version == "devel", ]
diverged_df <- do.call(rbind, lapply(regime_levels, function(r){
  x <- devel_df[devel_df$regime == r & !devel_df$is_de, ]

             frac_diverged = mean(x$nuisance > 1e4),

}))

6.4 The t → z mapping (NEWS: “no longer produces an infinite statistic”)

master computed the Gaussian statistic as qnorm(pt(T, df)), which returns Inf once pt() rounds to 1. devel works on the log scale. In these simulations master never reached Inf, because its capped nuisance rates keep its Welch statistics below about 26. Applying the old mapping to devel’s statistics shows where it would have failed:

tz_df <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("master", "devel"), function(v){
  x <- gene_df[gene_df$version == v, ]
  z_old_vec <- stats::qnorm(stats::pt(x$teststat, df = x$df))
  data.frame(version = v,
             max_teststat = max(x$teststat),
             num_inf_old_mapping = sum(!is.finite(z_old_vec)),
             num_nonfinite_reported = sum(!is.finite(x$gaussian_teststat)))
}))
knitr::kable(tz_df, digits = 1,
             col.names = c("Statistics from", "Largest Welch statistic",
                           "Inf under master's mapping",
                           "Non-finite z actually reported"),
             caption = "All 60 data sets.")
All 60 data sets.
Statistics from Largest Welch statistic Inf under master’s mapping Non-finite z actually reported
master 26.1 0 0
devel 52.9 10 0

So the log-scale mapping is a real fix, but the situation it guards against arises chiefly because of the other change: the uncapped nuisance rate produces the huge statistics.

devel records this; master does not (method is NA).

devel falls back from locfdr to the truncated MLE in a minority of replicates, most often in null and strong_de, and says so with a warning. master may have fallen back just as often; it had no way to report it.

7 Corner cases

Each row below perturbs one small cohort (10 individuals × 30 cells, 100 genes, 10 DE) and runs the full pipeline. “silent” means the pipeline finished without warnings.

case_vec <- unique(corner_df$case)
corner_wide_df <- do.call(rbind, lapply(case_vec, function(cs){
  m <- corner_df[corner_df$case == cs & corner_df$version == "master", ]
  d <- corner_df[corner_df$case == cs & corner_df$version == "devel", ]
  .describe <- function(x){
    txt <- x$outcome
    if(x$outcome == "error") txt <- paste0("**error** in ", x$error)
    if(x$outcome == "warning") txt <- paste0("warning: ", x$warnings)
    if(!is.na(x$num_sig)) txt <- paste0(txt, " — ", x$num_sig, " genes at FDR < 0.05")
    if(!is.na(x$metric_value)) txt <- paste0(txt, "; ", x$metric_name, " = ",
                                             signif(x$metric_value, 3))
    substr(txt, 1, 330)
  }
  data.frame(Case = paste0("`", cs, "`: ", d$description),
             master = .describe(m),
             devel = .describe(d))
}))
knitr::kable(corner_wide_df,
             caption = "Behavior of each version on the perturbed cohorts. Messages truncated.")

Case master devel

determinism: Same data, fitted after set.seed(1) and after set.seed(2) silent — 10 genes at FDR < 0.05; max |diff| in Welch statistic between the two fits = 4.4e-12 silent — 13 genes at FDR < 0.05; max |diff| in Welch statistic between the two fits = 0
sparse_input: Same counts as a dgCMatrix silent — 10 genes at FDR < 0.05; max |diff| in Welch statistic vs dense reference = 2.06e-11 silent — 13 genes at FDR < 0.05; max |diff| in Welch statistic vs dense reference = 0
sparse_na: One NA among the nonzero entries of a dgCMatrix error in initialize_esvd: missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed error in initialize_esvd: covariates contains NA or non-finite entries
all_zero_gene: Two genes are all-zero warning: from glmnet C++ code (error code -1); Convergence for 1th lambda value not reached after maxit=100000 iterations; solutions for larger lambdas returned || an empty model has been returned; probably a convergence issue — 9 genes at FDR < 0.05 error in initialize_esvd: 2 gene(s) are all zero (gene3, gene50); remove them before initialization, or run eSVD_helper, which removes them and records the removal in gene_status
collinear_covariate: A covariate column duplicated (Age twice) error in opt_esvd (first): missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed error in initialize_esvd: covariates is rank deficient (rank 5 for 6 columns): Age_copy can be written as a combination of the other columns. Remove one variable from each collinear set. Including an indicator for every individual, or for every level of a factor, causes this
confounded_design: Sex identical to case-control status error in opt_esvd (first): missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed error in initialize_esvd: covariates is rank deficient (rank 4 for 5 columns): Sex_M can be written as a combination of the other columns. Remove one variable from each collinear set. Including an indicator for every individual, or for every level of a factor, causes this
few_genes: Only 30 genes silent — 30 genes at FDR < 0.05 silent — 0 genes at FDR < 0.05
extreme_de: 5 genes up-regulated by exp(4), nearly Poisson silent — 5 genes at FDR < 0.05; largest Gaussian statistic = 5.04 warning: locfdr could not estimate the empirical null; using the truncated_mle estimator instead (null_mean = -3.337, null_sd = 1.534). This usually means too few genes for locfdr’s spline fit — 5 genes at FDR < 0.05; largest Gaussian statistic = 5.17
one_case_individual: The case arm has a single individual error in compute_pvalue: missing values and NaN’s not allowed if ‘na.rm’ is FALSE error in compute_test_statistic: each arm needs at least 2 individuals to form a two-sample test; found 1 case and 5 control. With one individual in an arm the Welch degrees of freedom are 0 and every p-value is NaN
two_cell_individual: One control individual has only 2 cells silent — 10 genes at FDR < 0.05 error in compute_test_statistic: individual(s) indiv1 (2 cells) have fewer than 3 cells. Remove them upstream (see eSVD_helper), or pass min_cells_per_individual = 0 to proceed anyway
individual_in_both_arms: Half of one individual’s cells labelled case, half control error in compute_test_statistic: length(intersect(control_individuals, case_individuals)) == 0 is not TRUE error in compute_test_statistic: length(intersect(control_individuals, case_individuals)) == 0 is not TRUE

Reading the table:

  • Fixed, and clearly better. collinear_covariate and confounded_design (Sex identical to case-control status) used to fail two stages later with missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed from opt_esvd(). Now they stop in initialize_esvd(), which names the redundant column. all_zero_gene used to finish with glmnet convergence warnings and fit the zero genes anyway; now it is refused by name and pointed at eSVD_helper(). one_case_individual used to die in compute_pvalue() on NaNs; now it stops in compute_test_statistic() with an explanation. two_cell_individual used to run silently; now it is refused (it can be overridden with min_cells_per_individual = 0).
  • few_genes is the most striking row. With 30 genes, master declared every gene significant, silently. Its unconstrained fallback estimator gave a degenerate empirical null. devel’s locfdr converged here and called nothing significant, which is conservative but at least not nonsense. (Across the head-to-head regimes devel does fall back in some replicates, and it warns when it does.)
  • Unchanged. individual_in_both_arms is refused by the same stopifnot() in both versions. The friendlier check lives in eSVD(), which these scripts do not call.
  • Not a practical difference in these data. determinism: master’s two fits after different set.seed() calls differed by about 1e-11 in the Welch statistic, so its random SVD start rarely mattered here; devel is bit-identical. sparse_input agrees with dense input in both.
  • sparse_na shows a gap between NEWS.md and behavior. NEWS says initialize_esvd() now zeroes NA counts in sparse matrices, but the pipeline never gets that far: format_covariates() computes Log_UMI = log(rowSums(dat)), which is NA for that cell, and initialize_esvd() then stops on the covariates. The error is clearer than master’s (covariates contains NA versus missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed), but it names the covariates rather than the count that caused them. The zeroing only helps a caller who builds the covariates some other way.
  • extreme_de (five genes up by \(e^4\) on nearly Poisson genes): both versions find the five genes. Neither overflowed at this size.

8 New in devel: a standard error for the log2 fold change

master has no counterpart. Below, the interval logFC ± 2 SE is checked against the true log2 fold change, split by whether the gene’s nuisance rate diverged.

se_df <- do.call(rbind, lapply(regime_levels, function(r){
  x <- devel_df[devel_df$regime == r, ]
  cover_vec <- abs(x$logFC - x$truth_log2fc) <= 2 * x$logFC_se
  diverged_vec <- x$nuisance > 1e4
  data.frame(regime = r,
             coverage_ordinary = mean(cover_vec[!diverged_vec]),
             coverage_diverged = ifelse(any(diverged_vec),
                                        mean(cover_vec[diverged_vec]), NA),
             median_se = stats::median(x$logFC_se))
}))
knitr::kable(se_df, digits = 3,
             col.names = c("Regime", "Coverage of ±2 SE, ordinary rate",
                           "Coverage of ±2 SE, diverged rate", "Median SE"),
             caption = "devel only, all genes and replicates.")
devel only, all genes and replicates.
Regime Coverage of ±2 SE, ordinary rate Coverage of ±2 SE, diverged rate Median SE
baseline 0.997 0.412 0.369
null 0.998 0.474 0.373
strong_de 0.835 0.000 0.382
near_poisson 1.000 0.415 0.335
minimal_design 1.000 0.455 0.368
generate_null 0.995 0.080 0.492 
plot_df <- devel_df[devel_df$regime == "baseline" & devel_df$rep == 1, ]
plot_df$diverged <- ifelse(plot_df$nuisance > 1e4, "rate diverged", "ordinary")
plot1 <- ggplot2::ggplot(plot_df, ggplot2::aes(x = truth_log2fc, y = logFC))
plot1 <- plot1 + ggplot2::geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0,
                                      colour = "#c3c2b7", linewidth = 0.5)
plot1 <- plot1 + ggplot2::geom_errorbar(ggplot2::aes(ymin = logFC - 2 * logFC_se,
                                                     ymax = logFC + 2 * logFC_se,
                                                     colour = diverged),
                                        width = 0, alpha = 0.5)
plot1 <- plot1 + ggplot2::geom_point(ggplot2::aes(colour = diverged), size = 1.2)
plot1 <- plot1 + ggplot2::scale_colour_manual(values = c(ordinary = "#2a78d6",
                                                         `rate diverged` = "#eb6834"),
                                              name = NULL)
plot1 <- plot1 + ggplot2::labs(x = "True log2 fold change",
                               y = "devel: log2 fold change ± 2 SE",
                               title = "baseline, replicate 1")
plot(plot1)

For genes with an ordinary nuisance estimate, the SE covers the truth at or above the nominal rate in five of the six regimes: it is conservative, as CLAUDE_kevin.md notes, because the within-individual term dominates. The exception is strong_de (coverage 0.84). There, the ±3 effects move each case cell’s total count, so the Log_UMI depth adjustment shifts every gene’s fold change. That is the bias recorded in CLAUDE_kevin.md, which an SE cannot absorb. For genes whose rate diverged, the interval collapses and coverage falls well below nominal. This is the same failure as in section 6, seen from the SE’s side.

10 Verdict

  • On the estimate researchers report first, the fold change, nothing changed.
  • On the test, one change is dramatic, and it is not a corner-case change. Uncapping gamma_rate gives nuisance rates that are more faithful in rank but biased upward, and occasionally divergent. That shrinks posterior variances and inflates Welch statistics. In ordinary regimes this costs a few false discoveries per 300 genes (from 0.2–1.8 up to 2.7–3.8 per data set). In low-overdispersion data it breaks calibration (type-I error 0.28 at p < 0.05). The ablation attributes all of it to this one change.
  • Everything else in NEWS.md behaves as a corner-case fix, and in those corners devel is clearly better: clear, early errors instead of deep crashes, and no silent “everything is significant” on small gene sets.

What this suggests for the CRAN release (Kevin’s decision; nothing here has been changed): the gamma_rate change needs either a guard or an upper bound before release. The bound would be a principled cap on \(\beta_j\), or a flag in report_results() for genes whose rate ran to the edge of the search. Q10 and Q-LFC-1 in CLAUDE_kevin.md are the open questions this data speaks to. The ablation machinery here (devel_swap) can test any candidate fix in about three minutes.

11 What we glossed over

  • Only simulated data, and mostly data from the eSVD model itself. The one outside generator (generate_null()) shows the same pattern in milder form. Real cohorts have thousands of genes, which helps locfdr and may change the size of the tail effect.
  • 300 genes, 20 individuals, 30 cells per individual. Chosen to fit the 30-minute budget. The false-discovery counts scale with the number of genes; the rates are what to compare.
  • eSVD() itself was not run, because it needs a Seurat object. The scripts call its steps in the same order and with its defaults, except k = 3 and max_iter = 50. compute_test_per_gene() (the bool_diet = TRUE path) was not compared.
  • The rescaling by bool_stabilize_underdispersion divides every rate by their geometric mean when that mean is above 1. It is on in both versions, and diverged genes inflate that mean under devel. Its separate contribution was not isolated.

  • Lin, K. Z., Qiu, Y., and Roeder, K. (2024). eSVD-DE: cohort-wide differential expression in single-cell RNA-seq data using exponential-family embeddings. BMC Bioinformatics 25:113. doi:10.1186/s12859-024-05724-7
